name: Coursera

Coursera Plus offers subscription access to thousands of courses and Specializations, and finishing a course can earn a shareable certificate, per Coursera's official pricing page (as of 2026-07-12)
Offers a genuine credential ladder — from certificates to industry Professional Certificates to fully online, accredited university degrees — so learners can pick the level that matches their goal
Many individual courses can be audited free, letting you evaluate the material before paying
cons: Coursera Plus does not cover everything: some Professional Certificates, Specializations, and all degree programs are priced separately, so the subscription is not an all-access pass to the full catalog

Advertised pricing is promotion-heavy and region-dependent, so the number you see may differ from the standard list price
best_for: Learners who want university- and industry-backed courses with a clear path from a certificate up to an accredited online degree.
summary: Coursera pairs the strongest academic provenance in this group — courses built with named universities and companies — with a real credential ladder from certificates to accredited degrees. The trade-offs are a subscription that doesn't cover degrees or every certificate, and promotion-heavy pricing.
verdict_summary: Coursera is our top overall pick because it combines documented academic provenance with a genuine credential ladder. Its content is developed with named universities and companies (Coursera's site lists 350+ partners), and the platform spans free-to-audit courses, subscription access through Coursera Plus, industry Professional Certificates, and fully online accredited university degrees — so a learner can match the credential to the goal. Coursera's official pricing page describes Coursera Plus as a monthly or annual subscription (about $59/month or $399/year US list price, as of 2026-07-12) that unlocks thousands of courses and Specializations, with certificates for courses you complete. The honest trade-offs: Coursera Plus explicitly does not include every Professional Certificate, Specialization, or any degree program, so it is not all-access; auditing usually withholds graded work and the certificate; and pricing is promotion-heavy and region-dependent. Note this rating reflects analysis of Coursera's published documentation, not an audit of learning outcomes. For breadth, provenance, and credentialing, Coursera leads.

faq.question: Does Coursera offer accredited degrees?

faq.question: What does Coursera Plus include?
faq.answer: Per Coursera's official pricing page, Coursera Plus is a monthly or annual subscription that unlocks thousands of courses and Specializations with a certificate for each course you complete. It does not include some Professional Certificates or Specializations, and it does not include degree programs (as of 2026-07-12).

Coursera hosts fully online degrees from partner universities alongside courses and certificates; degrees are conferred by the accredited institutions.

name: edX
price_summary: Most courses free to audit; verified certificates typically $50–$300 per course; multi-course programs priced higher (US pricing as of 2026-07-12; varies by course)
pros: Founded by MIT and Harvard and still hosts courses from many named universities, so academic provenance is strong and documented
Most courses can be audited for free, per edX's official help center, making it easy to try the material before paying
Offers verified certificates and stackable programs (MicroBachelors, MicroMasters, Professional Certificates) for learners who want a credential
Publishes financial assistance options for verified certificates, lowering the cost barrier for eligible learners
cons: Since edX was acquired by the for-profit company 2U in 2021, the audit experience has tightened on many courses — audit access windows can be time-limited and graded assignments and the certificate are withheld unless you pay
Verified-certificate pricing varies widely by course ($50–$300 is typical) and full programs can cost substantially more
Support and mentorship are lighter than a cohort bootcamp; the model is largely self-directed
best_for: Learners who want free access to university-created courses and the option to pay only when they need a verified credential.
summary: edX offers university-created courses — it was founded by MIT and Harvard — with most courses free to audit and paid verified certificates when you need a credential. The trade-offs are a tightened audit experience since the 2U acquisition and course-by-course certificate pricing.
verdict_summary: edX earns a high place on academic provenance and value. Founded by MIT and Harvard, it still hosts courses from many named universities, and its official help center confirms most courses can be audited for free — you pay only when you want the verified certificate, which typically runs $50–$300 per course, with larger stackable programs (MicroBachelors, MicroMasters, Professional Certificates) priced higher. edX also publishes financial-assistance options that can reduce verified-certificate costs for eligible learners. The honest trade-offs: since edX was acquired by the for-profit company 2U in 2021, the free audit experience has tightened on many courses — audit windows can be time-limited, and graded assignments and certificates are gated behind payment — and certificate pricing varies widely course to course. Support is largely self-directed rather than mentored. This rating analyzes edX's published documentation, not learning outcomes we measured. For free university-created content with an optional paid credential, edX is a strong, lower-cost choice.

faq.question: Is edX free?

faq.question: Who owns edX?
faq.answer: edX was founded by MIT and Harvard in 2012 as a nonprofit. In 2021 the edX platform was acquired by 2U, a for-profit education company, which now operates it. Courses are still created by partner universities and institutions.

faq.question: Can edX credentials count toward a degree?
faq.answer: Some edX programs, such as certain MicroMasters, are designed so that credit can be applied toward a related degree at a partner university if you are admitted. This varies by program and university, so confirm transfer terms with the institution before enrolling.

name: Khan Academy
price_summary: Completely free — Khan Academy is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by donations; no ads, no subscription (as of 2026-07-12)
pros: Completely free with no ads and no subscription — Khan Academy's help center states its materials are available for free and it is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by donations
Deep, standards-aligned coverage of math, science, and other academic subjects from preschool through early college, with videos, practice, and mastery tracking
Because it is a nonprofit with no ads, there is no upsell pressure and no monetization of learner attention
Excellent as a free supplement for K-12 and early-college coursework and for brushing up on fundamentals
cons: Khan Academy does not grant accredited degrees or widely recognized professional certificates, so it is a learning resource rather than a credentialing path — a real limitation if you need a credential for a job or transfer
Its focus is academic subjects (heavily math and science) rather than career or professional skills, so it is not a substitute for a bootcamp or professional course
Support is self-directed with limited instructor interaction; there are no cohorts, mentors, or graded human feedback
best_for: Students, parents, and self-learners who want genuinely free, high-quality academic instruction with no ads or upsells.
summary: Khan Academy is the best free option here: a 501(c)(3) nonprofit offering ad-free, standards-aligned academic instruction from preschool through early college. Its clear limitation is credentialing — it grants no accredited degrees or professional certificates.
verdict_summary: Khan Academy is unmatched on cost and academic value, which is why it ranks this high despite offering no credential. Its help center confirms it is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit whose materials are free, with no ads and no subscription, funded by donations. The content is deep and standards-aligned — math, science, and other academic subjects from preschool through early college, with instructional videos, practice, and mastery tracking. Because it is a nonprofit with no advertising, there is no upsell and no monetization of learner attention. The honest limitation is credentialing and scope: Khan Academy does not grant accredited degrees or widely recognized professional certificates, so it is a learning resource rather than a path to a job-ready credential, and its focus is academic subjects rather than professional skills. Support is self-directed with limited human feedback. This rating analyzes Khan Academy's published documentation, not outcomes we measured. As a free academic supplement, nothing here beats it; as a credentialing path, look elsewhere.

pricing_table.notes: All learning content is free with no ads and no subscription. Khan Academy is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit funded by donors and grants.

faq.question: Is Khan Academy really free?
faq.answer: Yes. Khan Academy's help center states its materials are available for free, with no contracts, no spam, and no ads, and that it is a 501(c)(3) not-for-profit organization funded by donations and grants (as of 2026-07-12).

faq.question: Does Khan Academy offer a degree or accredited certificate?
faq.answer: No. Khan Academy provides free instructional content and practice, not accredited degrees or widely recognized professional certificates. It is best used as a free learning and review resource rather than a credentialing path.

faq.question: What subjects does Khan Academy cover?
faq.answer: Khan Academy focuses on standards-aligned academic subjects — heavily math and science, plus others — from preschool through early college. It is not oriented toward career or professional-skills training the way a bootcamp or professional course platform is.

evidence_points.claim: Khan Academy's materials are free with no ads, and it is a 501(c)(3) not-for-profit organization funded by donations.

verdict_summary: LinkedIn Learning is a practical choice for working professionals building job skills. Its catalog covers software, business, management, and creative topics taught by industry practitioners, and finishing a course produces a certificate of completion you can display on your LinkedIn profile. LinkedIn's documentation describes an individual subscription billed monthly or annually (about $239.88/year, roughly $19.99/month billed annually, with a higher month-to-month rate) plus a one-month free trial, and the service is included at no extra charge with LinkedIn Premium — so many professionals already have it. name: Udemy

pros: Enormous catalog spanning almost any practical topic, with lifetime access to individual courses you purchase (per Udemy's course model)
Individual courses are frequently discounted heavily, so a specific skill can be very inexpensive to pick up
An optional Personal Plan subscription bundles access to a large selection of courses for a monthly or annual fee

cons: Udemy is an open marketplace where almost anyone can publish a course, so quality is highly variable from course to course — the single biggest caveat, and it means you must vet each instructor and course individually rather than trust the platform name
Courses are not accredited and do not carry recognized academic or professional credentials
List prices are heavily promotion-driven; the 'original' price is often far above what courses actually sell for, so headline discounts can be misleading
best_for: Self-directed learners who want an inexpensive, on-demand way to pick up a specific practical skill and are willing to vet individual courses.
summary: Udemy is a vast, inexpensive marketplace for picking up specific practical skills, with lifetime access to purchased courses and frequent discounts. The central caveat is quality: it is an open marketplace, so course quality varies widely and you must vet each one.
verdict_summary: Udemy is the go-to marketplace for inexpensively picking up a specific, practical skill. Its catalog is enormous, individual courses come with lifetime access once purchased, and prices are frequently discounted, so a targeted skill can cost very little. An optional Personal Plan subscription bundles a large course selection for a monthly or annual fee, and most course purchases carry a 30-day refund policy per Udemy's documentation. The central, documentable caveat is quality control: Udemy is an open marketplace where almost anyone can become an instructor and publish a course, so quality varies widely from course to course — you must vet each instructor and course individually rather than trust the platform name. Courses are also not accredited, and list prices are heavily promotion-driven, so headline 'discounts' can be misleading. This rating analyzes Udemy's published model and policies, not outcomes we measured. For cheap, self-directed, skill-specific learning — with careful vetting — Udemy delivers.

Its lessons are conversation-first but also teach explicit grammar, organized in a clear beginner-to-advanced path and developed by language-teaching experts — a good fit for learners who want to understand the language, not just drill vocabulary. name: Duolingo
price_summary: Free tier with ads; Super Duolingo (ad-free) about $12.99/month or $95.99/year; Duolingo Max (adds AI features) about $29.99/month or $167.99/year; Family plan about $119.99/year for up to 6 (US list price as of 2026-07-12; varies by region and promotions)
pros: Genuinely capable free tier — you can learn a language without paying, which no other app here matches at this scale
Short, gamified lessons with streaks and reminders make it easy to build a daily habit across many languages

cons: The free tier is ad-supported and includes interruptions and (historically) limits like hearts, which the paid Super tier removes — so the free experience is deliberately friction-laden

Its bite-sized, translation-and-recognition style builds vocabulary and habit well but provides limited real conversational and speaking practice, so it is better as a supplement than a sole path to fluency
Duolingo Max's headline AI features cost roughly double Super, and some previously Max-only features have shifted over time, so weigh what you actually get
best_for: Beginners and casual learners who want a free, habit-building way to start a language across many options.
summary: Duolingo's standout is a genuinely useful free tier and habit-building, gamified lessons across many languages. Its limits: ads and friction on the free tier, and limited real speaking practice in its core format.
verdict_summary: Duolingo's defining strength is access: its free tier is genuinely capable, letting you learn a language without paying — something no other app here matches at this scale — with short, gamified lessons and reminders that make a daily habit easy across many languages. Paid tiers layer on top: Super Duolingo removes ads and adds practice features (about $12.99/month or $95.99/year), Duolingo Max adds AI-driven features (about $29.99/month or $167.99/year), and a Family plan covers up to six people for about $119.99/year (US list prices as of 2026-07-12, varying by region and promotions). The honest trade-offs: the free tier is ad-supported and deliberately friction-laden to nudge upgrades; the core translation-and-recognition style builds vocabulary and habit but offers limited real conversational and speaking practice, so it works best as a supplement rather than a sole route to fluency; and Max costs roughly double Super. This rating analyzes Duolingo's published documentation, not any efficacy study. For a free, low-friction start, Duolingo is hard to beat.

faq.answer: Yes — Duolingo has a genuinely usable free tier supported by ads and some usage limits, which is its biggest advantage among these apps. Paid Super and Max tiers remove ads and add features (as of 2026-07-12).

faq.question: What is the difference between Super and Max?
faq.answer: Super Duolingo removes ads and adds practice features (about $12.99/month or $95.99/year). Duolingo Max adds AI-powered features on top of Super and costs roughly double (about $29.99/month or $167.99/year). A Family plan covers up to six people for about $119.99/year (US list prices as of 2026-07-12).

faq.question: Can Duolingo make me fluent?
faq.answer: Duolingo is strong for building vocabulary and a daily habit, but its bite-sized, translation-and-recognition format offers limited real conversational and speaking practice. It is best used as a supplement alongside speaking practice rather than a sole path to fluency.

evidence_points.claim: Duolingo offers a free ad-supported tier plus paid Super (ad-free) and Max (AI features) subscriptions and a Family plan.

verdict_summary: Rosetta Stone is the long-established name in immersion learning: it teaches through images and target-language context rather than translation, aiming to build intuition the way you'd pick up a language by exposure. Its TruAccent speech-recognition feature scores your pronunciation and nudges it toward clearer delivery, per Rosetta Stone's documentation. Pricing centers on a 12-month single-language subscription around $143.40 and a Lifetime (all languages) plan listed near $399 but frequently discounted to roughly $179–$219, with a 3-day free trial and a 30-day money-back guarantee (US list prices as of 2026-07-12, promotion-dependent). The honest trade-offs: the immersion method deliberately minimizes explicit grammar explanation and translation, which frustrates adult learners who want a rule stated plainly; the Lifetime list price is high and the good price depends on promotions rather than a stable rate; and TruAccent is automated scoring, not human correction, so it can't explain nuance the way a teacher or a community feature can. This rating analyzes Rosetta Stone's published documentation, not any efficacy study. For immersion-style learning with pronunciation feedback, it fits a specific preference.

faq.question: How does Rosetta Stone teach?
faq.answer: Through immersion: lessons pair images with the target language and largely avoid translation and explicit grammar rules, so you infer meaning from context. Its TruAccent feature adds automated speech-recognition feedback on pronunciation (as of 2026-07-12).

faq.question: Does Rosetta Stone explain grammar?
faq.answer: Only lightly. The immersion method deliberately minimizes explicit grammar explanation and native-language translation. Learners who want rules explained directly often find this frustrating and may need to supplement with a grammar-focused resource.

faq.question: Is the Lifetime plan worth it?
faq.answer: It depends on price and commitment. The Lifetime (all languages) plan lists near $399 but is frequently discounted to roughly $179–$219; at the discounted price it can be economical for committed multi-language learners, but the good price depends on catching a promotion (US list prices as of 2026-07-12).

evidence_points.claim: Rosetta Stone sells subscription and Lifetime plans and includes TruAccent speech-recognition pronunciation feedback in its immersion courses.
